title: TLS 1.3 & The Future of HTTPS 🚀
description: Discover the speed and security improvements in TLS 1.3 and what’s next.

slides.title: What’s New in TLS 1.3? ⚡
slides.content:
# TLS 1.3 is a major redesign for speed and security.

Key improvements:
- **Reduced handshake** – 1‑RTT (instead of 2), sometimes 0‑RTT for resumed connections.
- **Only forward‑secure key exchanges** – DHE and ECDHE mandatory; RSA key transport removed.
- **Simpler cipher suites** – only 5 AEAD suites (AES‑GCM, ChaCha20‑Poly1305).
- **Encrypted handshake** – the Server Certificate and other messages are encrypted, improving privacy.
- **Removal of dangerous features** – renegotiation, compression, static RSA, CBC mode.

slides.title: The 1‑RTT Handshake (simplified) 🚄
slides.content:
# 1. ClientHello includes a key share (client’s ephemeral ECDH public key) right away.
2. Server replies with ServerHello + its key share + encrypted Certificate & Finished.
3. Client finishes with its encrypted Finished.

By the time the server sends its first response, secure data can be sent simultaneously. This cuts a full round trip.

With 0‑RTT (using a pre‑shared key from a previous session), data can be sent in the first packet – but with some replay risk.

quizData.question: What enables 0‑RTT in TLS 1.3?

options.text: A pre‑shared key from a previous session

quizData.explanation: 0‑RTT uses a PSK (Pre‑Shared Key) established in an earlier session to immediately start sending data.

slides.title: Encrypted SNI (ESNI) & Privacy 🕶️
slides.content:
# The Server Name Indication (SNI) tells the server which host the client wants, sent in ClientHello. In TLS 1.2, SNI is in plaintext, so a network observer can see which sites you visit even if the traffic is encrypted.

**Encrypted SNI (ESNI)** / **Encrypted ClientHello (ECH)** in TLS 1.3 encrypts the SNI, hiding the destination from snoopers.

Combined with DNS‑over‑HTTPS, this makes censorship and surveillance much harder.

slides.title: Post‑Quantum TLS 🧬
slides.content:
# Large‑scale quantum computers could break RSA and ECC. The TLS ecosystem is preparing:

- NIST is standardising post‑quantum algorithms (lattice‑based, code‑based, etc.).
- Experiments already integrate post‑quantum key exchange (e.g., CRYSTALS‑Kyber) into TLS handshake alongside classical ECDHE.
- Hybrid mode: use both classical and PQ key exchange, so security holds if either is secure.

TLS 1.3 can already negotiate these experimental algorithms. Migration will be gradual.

slides.title: Stay Up to Date 📆
slides.content: ## Always run the latest TLS libraries (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, etc.) with secure defaults. Test your servers with SSL Labs to catch weak configurations.

quizData.question: TLS 1.3 supports RSA key transport as an option for backward compatibility.
quizData.explanation: False. RSA key transport has been removed entirely from TLS 1.3; only forward‑secure methods remain.
